Pregnancy

13 to 16 Weeks Pregnant: Second Trimester Start Guide

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

At 16 weeks pregnant, your baby is about the size of an avocado, and many parents notice more energy, less nausea, and the first round ligament twinges as the uterus rises out of the pelvis. Weeks 13 to 16 are the opening stretch of the second trimester, a window when appointments settle into a rhythm and a few optional tests come up. This guide walks through what is growing, how you might feel, and what is worth doing now.

Your baby, from a lemon to an avocado

At 13 weeks, your baby is about the size of a lemon, roughly 7 centimeters from head to bottom. Over the next few weeks that length nearly doubles. At 14 weeks the kidneys are producing urine, the neck is lengthening, and facial muscles are starting to work, so your baby can squint and grimace. Fine, soft hair called lanugo begins to cover the skin, and the arms grow to a length that better matches the body. None of this is visible from the outside yet, which can feel strange. Growth in this window is fast, steady, and mostly quiet.

By 15 to 16 weeks, your baby is about the size of an avocado, around 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump. Sucking motions begin, a rehearsal for feeding later. The ears have moved close to their final position, and the eyes have begun to make slow movements even though the eyelids stay fused. On an ultrasound around this time, the sex may be visible, although position and image quality decide whether the sonographer can say anything with confidence. Some parents feel the first faint flutters near 16 weeks, but many feel nothing until 18 to 22 weeks, especially in a first pregnancy. Both are normal.

How you might feel from week 13 to 16

For many people, this stretch is when pregnancy finally starts to feel easier. Nausea fades for a large share of parents somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks, appetite comes back, and energy often returns as first trimester exhaustion lifts. The shift is real but not universal. Some people stay queasy into the second trimester, and a smaller group deals with nausea for much longer. If you are still vomiting often, cannot keep fluids down, or are losing weight, tell your clinician rather than waiting for it to pass. There is treatment for persistent nausea, and asking for it is not a failure.

New sensations arrive as your uterus rises up and out of the pelvis. Round ligament pain often starts in this window: quick, sharp twinges low in the belly or groin when you stand, cough, sneeze, or roll over in bed. It is common and usually brief, and our round ligament pain guide covers relief in detail. You may also notice a firmer lower belly, nasal stuffiness, gum tenderness, and mild lightheadedness when you get up quickly, all tied to extra blood flow. A visible bump follows its own schedule, which our guide on when you start showing explains, so try not to compare yourself with others.

Appointments and tests in this window

Prenatal visits usually settle into a rhythm of roughly every four weeks through the middle of pregnancy, as long as things are going smoothly. Expect the basics at each visit: blood pressure, weight, urine checks, and listening to the fetal heartbeat with a handheld Doppler. These weeks sit just after the first trimester screening window, so if you had that testing, this is often when results are discussed. Because the second trimester officially begins around this point, a topic our trimesters guide covers, many clinics also use these visits to plan the rest of your testing calendar. Bring questions written down; short visits go faster than expected.

Two tests belong to this stretch. The quad screen, a blood test that estimates the chance of neural tube defects and certain chromosomal conditions, including Down syndrome, is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is optional, and it is a screening test, not a diagnosis. Amniocentesis, when it is indicated by screening results, family history, or your own preference after counseling, is usually performed between about 15 and 20 weeks. If either test is on your mind, raise it at your next visit so the calendar does not decide for you.

Good things to do between 13 and 16 weeks

Book the anatomy scan now if your clinic has not already scheduled it. This detailed ultrasound usually happens between 18 and 22 weeks, and appointment slots can fill early, especially if you want a particular day or time. It is also a sensible moment to plan travel. Many people find the middle weeks of pregnancy the most comfortable for a trip: nausea has often faded, the bump is still small, and energy is better. Check your travel insurance, pack a copy of your prenatal records, and ask your clinician about anything specific to the destination, such as long flights, altitude, or food and water safety.

If energy is returning, put some of it into gentle movement such as walking, swimming, or prenatal yoga; our safe exercise guide covers what to choose and what to skip. This is also a good window for unglamorous logistics: check parental leave paperwork deadlines, start a short list of questions for the anatomy scan, and note symptoms or dates somewhere you will actually find them later, whether that is a notebook or the BeMama app. Small habits started now, like a consistent bedtime and a water bottle you refill all day, tend to matter more in the third trimester than any single burst of preparation.

When to call your clinician

Call promptly for bleeding that is more than light spotting, fluid leaking from the vagina, a fever of 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, severe or one-sided abdominal pain, pain or burning when you urinate, or vomiting that keeps you from holding down fluids. These signs do not automatically mean something is wrong, but each one deserves a same-day conversation rather than a search engine. Heavy bleeding that soaks a pad in an hour, severe pain that does not ease, fainting, or trouble breathing calls for emergency care right away, not a message and a wait. If you notice spotting after sex or a pelvic exam, mention that too; it is often harmless, and your clinician can tell you what to watch for. Save the office number and the after-hours line in your phone now, before you need them.

Mood deserves the same attention as physical symptoms. Relief and excitement often grow in these weeks, but anxiety, low mood, or intrusive worry can grow too, and pregnancy hormones are not a reason to dismiss them. Tell your clinician if sadness or worry fills most of the day for more than two weeks, disturbs your sleep beyond ordinary discomfort, or makes it hard to eat or function. Support ranges from talk therapy to medication that can be used in pregnancy, and any thoughts of harming yourself deserve immediate help from a crisis line or your care team, not a wait for the next appointment. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis; your own care team knows your history and is the right place for personal answers.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Pregnancy is dated from the first day of the last menstrual period and is commonly described in weeks and trimesters. ACOG’s week ranges describe typical development, but they are an orientation rather than a test of an individual fetus.

Due dates are estimates, and ultrasound is used for medical reasons to assess gestational age, growth, anatomy, position, and other questions. Only a qualified prenatal professional can interpret findings for a specific pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama’s week view for education, appointment preparation, and dated notes. It cannot confirm fetal growth, anatomy, heartbeat, or wellbeing.

When to seek help

Contact your prenatal team for bleeding, severe pain, fluid leakage, reduced movement after movement is established, or any urgent concern instead of relying on a week-by-week article.

Key takeaways

  • Your baby grows from about a lemon to an avocado between 13 and 16 weeks.
  • Energy often returns and nausea fades for many people, but not for everyone.
  • Round ligament twinges commonly begin as the uterus rises out of the pelvis.
  • The quad screen is offered at about 15 to 22 weeks, and the anatomy scan should be booked for 18 to 22 weeks.
  • Call your clinician the same day for bleeding, leaking fluid, or fever.

Frequently asked questions

How big is baby at 16 weeks?

At 16 weeks, a baby is about the size of an avocado, roughly 11 to 12 centimeters from crown to rump and around 100 grams. Ultrasound measurements normally vary a little from these averages. A steady growth pattern over time matters more than any single number on a report.

What weeks is the quad screen done?

The quad screen is offered between about 15 and 22 weeks of pregnancy, and many clinics aim for 16 to 18 weeks. It is an optional blood test that estimates the chance of certain conditions rather than diagnosing them. If a result is flagged, your clinician will walk you through follow-up options such as detailed ultrasound or amniocentesis.

When does round ligament pain start?

Round ligament pain most often starts in the early second trimester, around 13 to 16 weeks, as the uterus rises out of the pelvis and its supporting ligaments stretch. The twinges are typically sharp, brief, and set off by sudden movement like standing, coughing, or rolling over. Pain that is severe, constant, or paired with bleeding or fever is not typical round ligament pain, so call your clinician.

Do you feel better in the second trimester?

Many people do feel better in the second trimester, with nausea fading, energy returning, and appetite improving, often somewhere between 13 and 16 weeks. The change is gradual rather than a switch flipping on a set day. If you still feel rough at 16 weeks, that is common too, and persistent vomiting or exhaustion is worth raising at your next visit.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
